			</item>
		<item>
		<title>Lucy Sparrow Invokes &#8217;90s Supermarket Nostalgia in ‘The Beginning of Convenience’</title>
		<link>https://www.thisiscolossal.com/2026/07/lucy-sparrow-the-beginning-of-convenience/</link>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Jackie Andres]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Tue, 28 Jul 2026 20:11:28 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Art]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Craft]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[consumerism]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[felt]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[installation]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Lucy Sparrow]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[sewing]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[textiles]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://www.thisiscolossal.com/?p=476119</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[<p><img src="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/sparrow-boc-10.jpg" alt="Lucy Sparrow Invokes &#8217;90s Supermarket Nostalgia in ‘The Beginning of Convenience’" />The artist's new exhibition is fully stocked with more than 20,000 handmade felt objects.</p>
<p>Do stories and artists like this matter to you? Become a <a href="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/members">Colossal Member</a> today and support independent arts publishing for as little as $7 per month. The article <a href="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/2026/07/lucy-sparrow-the-beginning-of-convenience/">Lucy Sparrow Invokes &#8217;90s Supermarket Nostalgia in ‘The Beginning of Convenience’</a> appeared first on <a href="https://www.thisiscolossal.com">Colossal</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<img src="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/sparrow-boc-10.jpg" alt="Lucy Sparrow Invokes &#8217;90s Supermarket Nostalgia in ‘The Beginning of Convenience’" />


<p>Bentonville is a small town in Northwest Arkansas that has, over time, become synonymous with massive retail operations and corporate ecosystems. The bustling hub is ingrained with the legacy of <a href="https://downtownbentonville.org/go/the-walton-5-and-10" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">Walton&#8217;s</a>, a small nickel and dime convenience store that opened on Bentonville&#8217;s downtown square in 1950 to serve its surrounding community. The shop quickly found success, and owner Sam Walton opened another store nearby that would evolve into the <a href="https://corporate.walmart.com/about/history" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">largest retailer</a> in the world: Walmart.</p>



<p>During this time and throughout the &#8217;60s, a post-war boom overtook the burgeoning commercial landscape of the United States. The suburban American Dream became a catalyst for retailers to adapt to an evolving social fabric that aimed to serve families hunting for necessities at an affordable price, and in a pinch. As a result, various amenities were introduced to convenience stores and chains, including the emergence of <a href="https://www.convenience.org/topics/fuels-and-energy/the-history-of-self-fueling" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">self-serve gasoline pumps</a>.</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image"><img loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="2000" height="1333" src="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/sparrow-boc-12.jpg" alt="a collection of handmade felt plush sculptures by Lucy Sparrow replicating a supermarket aisle stocked with various products and produce" class="wp-image-476178" srcset="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/sparrow-boc-12.jpg 2000w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/sparrow-boc-12-640x427.jpg 640w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/sparrow-boc-12-960x640.jpg 960w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/sparrow-boc-12-768x512.jpg 768w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/sparrow-boc-12-1536x1024.jpg 1536w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 2000px) 100vw, 2000px" /><figcaption class="wp-element-caption">Installation view of &#8216;The Beginning of Convenience.&#8217; Photo by Wesley Hitt, courtesy of Getty Images for The Momentary</figcaption></figure>



<p>The 1980s and &#8217;90s, however, ushered in a new frontier of American commerce rooted in modernization. Supermarkets began to resemble the eptiome of a &#8220;one-stop-shop,&#8221; significantly transcending previous notions of convenience. In just one trip to the store, busy parents had the ability to pick out groceries for the week, restock housekeeping supplies, fill prescriptions, and feed their families lunch at the food court—all while waiting for their vacation photos to develop via <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/1988/02/06/business/rapid-rise-of-fast-photo-processing.html?unlocked_article_code=1.1FA.2GYn.1I9gFKNFfPHJ&amp;smid=url-share" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">rapid film processing</a>. Securing a quick and easy premade dinner was possible thanks to the popular frozen food aisle, and as a cherry on top, VHS movies were available for purchase to pair with the titular &#8220;<a href="https://www.smithsonianmag.com/arts-culture/brief-history-tv-dinner-180976039/" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">TV dinner</a>.&#8221;</p>



<p>U.K.-based artist <a href="https://www.sewyoursoul.co.uk/" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">Lucy Sparrow</a> refers to this moment as &#8220;the beginning of convenience,&#8221; which doubles as the title of her newest large-scale installation and first museum exhibition in the United States. <em>The Beginning of Convenience</em> at <a href="https://themomentary.org/" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">The Momentary</a> calls to the nostalgia of regional chain stores, retro packaging aesthetics, and a time when life was, as the artist described at the show&#8217;s opening, &#8220;becoming more about enjoyment and less about toil.&#8221;</p>



<p>For many, modern grocery stores can be imposing, and Sparrow&#8217;s monumental assemblage conjures a similar feeling of being carried away. The immensity of <em>The Beginning of Convenience</em>, however, invokes feelings of joy and comfort, rather than a newfangled sensory overload. Stocked to the brim with more than 20,000 handmade objects, an expansive collection of soft, felt artworks take over a 4,000-square-foot gallery space, creating an immersive experience for visitors—or, more fittingly—shoppers.</p>



<p>Much of the magic comes from the painstaking details that work together in molding an all-out sensory experience. For instance, as viewers weave through the aisles, music in the <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sXghfBU5EWY" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">style of old-school supermarket beats</a> hums in the background. The music however, is occasionally interrupted with amusing, familiar intercom announcements in a fuzzy tone, calling the parents or guardians of a lost young girl named Lucy to make their way to the photo department.</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image"><img loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="2000" height="1333" src="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/sparrow-boc-1.jpg" alt="a collection of handmade felt plush sculptures by Lucy Sparrow replicating VHS tapes of iconic movies" class="wp-image-476167" srcset="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/sparrow-boc-1.jpg 2000w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/sparrow-boc-1-640x427.jpg 640w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/sparrow-boc-1-960x640.jpg 960w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/sparrow-boc-1-768x512.jpg 768w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/sparrow-boc-1-1536x1024.jpg 1536w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 2000px) 100vw, 2000px" /><figcaption class="wp-element-caption">Installation view of &#8216;The Beginning of Convenience.&#8217; Photo by Wesley Hitt, courtesy of Getty Images for The Momentary</figcaption></figure>



<p>At the opening earlier this month, the artist was dressed for the occasion wearing a light blue, collared button-down shirtdress with vertical stripes running down the middle. Sparrow and her team shared that the custom garment was inspired by original Walmart uniforms from the company&#8217;s archives, extending a subtle nod to the fitting location of the exhibition.</p>



<p>Sparrow wields a remarkable ability to craft welcoming spaces for quite literally anyone. Each of the artist&#8217;s renowned <a href="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/tags/lucy-sparrow/">installations over the years</a> are the brainchild of her own imaginative world, and a sense of vulnerability comes with our invitation into it. &#8220;Lucy’s work is quirky yet subversive,” says an exhibition statement. “Her soft and colorful felt creations charm and disarm visitors, while her detailed research practice and incisive observations inspire strong feelings of nostalgia, community, and conversations around shared history.”</p>



<p>This deeply humane feeling is refreshing within the context of American consumerism and growing corporatism. Especially as of late, the simple task of grocery shopping has become an increasingly divisive experience, and for many Americans, trips to the store are a looming reminder of shrinking household budgets and soaring prices, making it difficult to associate ordinary retail environments with anything but exhaustion or stress.</p>



<p>The presence of joy and childlike wonder in <em>The Beginning of Convenience</em> offers a significant subversion. Injecting this feeling into a visceral environment allows each viewer to shift their focus to enjoyment, the marvels of retail innovation, and the nostalgia that comes with it.</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="960" height="1132" src="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/lucy-jackiesphone-1-960x1132.jpg" alt="boxes of fruit with smiling faces" class="wp-image-476234" srcset="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/lucy-jackiesphone-1-960x1132.jpg 960w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/lucy-jackiesphone-1-640x755.jpg 640w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/lucy-jackiesphone-1-768x905.jpg 768w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/lucy-jackiesphone-1-1303x1536.jpg 1303w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/lucy-jackiesphone-1-1737x2048.jpg 1737w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/lucy-jackiesphone-1.jpg 2000w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 960px) 100vw, 960px" /><figcaption class="wp-element-caption">Installation view of &#8216;The Beginning of Convenience.&#8217; Photo by Jackie Andres</figcaption></figure>



<p>Evoking the emotional power of soft toys, felt as a material inspires feelings of warmth and security. While walking through Sparrow&#8217;s produce and meat department, this impression seems nearly impossible to ignore as netted bags of oranges, piles of juicy grapefruits, and fresh cuts of pork chop look up at you with shy smiles.</p>



<p>Because of this, it seems easy to tap into an imaginative world where many of Sparrow&#8217;s plush products unmistakably possess individual souls. Perhaps the Georgia peaches have a more bubbly personality than their spiky pineapple neighbors, and, conceivably, the beef steaks across the aisle may be tough on the outside but tender at heart. Somehow anything seems possible in a world that melds the energetic spirit of commercialism with the with the slow, mindful creation of the same objects through cutting, stuffing, sewing, and embellishing.</p>



<p>Upon exiting the supermarket experience, viewers encounter even more felt versions of common items within grocery store vestibules: vending machines dispensing your choice of Coke or Pepsi products, a photobooth, a coin-operated mechanical car ride, and an electronic ATM, which, at the time, was reaching its ubiquity.</p>



<p>Turning the corner into a separate area, visitors are met with a massive floor-to-ceiling installation of more than 3,000 stuffed bananas. The sight is a recreation of the artist&#8217;s &#8220;Banana Room,&#8221; a comforting place in her studio to relax and &#8220;be surrounded by happiness,&#8221; she says. Sparrow received her first plush banana when she was nine years old as a present from her father, and later received a larger version who was named Sebastian. Sebastian&#8217;s presence throughout the show and as a mascot for the artist&#8217;s practice is further proof of the unfaltering childlike wonder imbued within every corner of Sparrow&#8217;s practice.</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image"><img loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="2000" height="1333" src="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/sparrow-boc-6.jpg" alt="Luct Sparrow sits in a room filled with thousands of bananas" class="wp-image-476172" srcset="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/sparrow-boc-6.jpg 2000w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/sparrow-boc-6-640x427.jpg 640w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/sparrow-boc-6-960x640.jpg 960w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/sparrow-boc-6-768x512.jpg 768w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/sparrow-boc-6-1536x1024.jpg 1536w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 2000px) 100vw, 2000px" /><figcaption class="wp-element-caption">Lucy Sparrow at &#8216;The Beginning of Convenience.&#8217; Photo by Wesley Hitt, courtesy of Getty Images for The Momentary</figcaption></figure>



<p>Across from the Banana Room sits a replica of the &#8220;Felt Cave.&#8221; The space—previously an ambulance station that was converted into Sparrow&#8217;s Suffolk studio—offers more insight into her artistic process and the <a href="https://www.sewyoursoul.co.uk/inside-felt-hq/" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">teamwork</a> that goes into creating thousands of objects, one at a time. Sparrow is supported by five full-time assistants, four cats, freelancers, and, of course, Sebastian.</p>



<p>Along with a faux window displaying the exact view from the studio—overlooking two colorful cars frequently parked outside, including a hot pink Jeep sporting a &#8220;F3LT U&#8221; license plate—The Felt Cave is filled with hundreds more surprises. As the exhibition label notes, there is &#8220;an &#8216;HR Department&#8217; of bespectacled bananas, a canary yellow cuckoo clock, and &#8216;dab dabs&#8217;—abstract paintings created from dabbing the excess off the tip of a paint bottle.&#8221;</p>



<p><em>The Beginning of Convenience</em> is on view through July 11, 2027. </p>



<figure class="wp-block-image"><img loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="2000" height="1333" src="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/sparrow-boc-5.jpg" alt="a collection of handmade felt plush sculptures by Lucy Sparrow replicating a supermarket aisle stocked with various products and produce" class="wp-image-476171" srcset="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/sparrow-boc-5.jpg 2000w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/sparrow-boc-5-640x427.jpg 640w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/sparrow-boc-5-960x640.jpg 960w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/sparrow-boc-5-768x512.jpg 768w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/sparrow-boc-5-1536x1024.jpg 1536w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 2000px) 100vw, 2000px" /><figcaption class="wp-element-caption">Installation view of &#8216;The Beginning of Convenience.&#8217; Photo by Wesley Hitt, courtesy of Getty Images for The Momentary</figcaption></figure>

		<title>Nature or Culture? Europeans Can Vote on the New Banknote Design</title>
		<link>https://www.thisiscolossal.com/2026/07/euro-banknote-design-central-bank/</link>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Grace Ebert]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Tue, 28 Jul 2026 14:21:05 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Design]]></category>

					<description><![CDATA[<p><img src="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/euro-3.jpeg" alt="Nature or Culture? Europeans Can Vote on the New Banknote Design" />Birds or figures? These are the ten design proposals for a new European banknote.</p>
<p>Do stories and artists like this matter to you? Become a <a href="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/members">Colossal Member</a> today and support independent arts publishing for as little as $7 per month. Europeans Can Vote on the New Banknote Design</a> appeared first on <a href="https://www.thisiscolossal.com">Colossal</a>.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<img src="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/euro-3.jpeg" alt="Nature or Culture? Europeans Can Vote on the New Banknote Design" />


<p>What best represents European life? The eternal dichotomy of nature vs. culture structures the Central Bank&#8217;s quest for a new banknote design, and now, the public can vote and offer feedback on ten proposals. </p>



<p>A panel of jurors selected the designs, which follow one of two themes: European places and ideas or birds and rivers, the latter of which is meant to symbolize freedom and unity. While the basic elements are the same—all collections devoted to culture feature the same six figures, including Renaissance artist Leonardo da Vinci, composer Ludwig van Beethoven, scientist Marie Curie, opera singer Maria Callas, and authors Bertha von Suttner and Miguel de Cervantes, for example—individual approaches appear in the layout, aesthetic, and composition.</p>



<p>Voting is open through mid-September, when jurors will select one design that will go through an additional vetting process before the organization adopts it entirely. View all ten on <a href="https://www.ecb.europa.eu/euro/banknotes/future_banknotes/html/all-design-proposals.en.html" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">the bank&#8217;s website</a>.</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-full"><img loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="2000" height="1177" src="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/euro-4.jpg" alt="a collection of potential designs for euros" class="wp-image-476224" srcset="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/euro-4.jpg 2000w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/euro-4-640x377.jpg 640w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/euro-4-960x565.jpg 960w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/euro-4-768x452.jpg 768w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/euro-4-1536x904.jpg 1536w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 2000px) 100vw, 2000px" /><figcaption class="wp-element-caption">Rudy Guedj and François Girard-Meunier</figcaption></figure>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-full"><img loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="2000" height="1215" src="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/euro-5.jpg" alt="a collection of potential designs for euros" class="wp-image-476226" srcset="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/euro-5.jpg 2000w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/euro-5-640x389.jpg 640w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/euro-5-960x583.jpg 960w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/euro-5-768x467.jpg 768w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/euro-5-1536x933.jpg 1536w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 2000px) 100vw, 2000px" /><figcaption class="wp-element-caption">Neue Gestaltung GmbH</figcaption></figure>

<figure class="wp-block-image size-full"><img loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="2000" height="1137" src="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/eruo-2.jpg" alt="a collection of potential designs for euros" class="wp-image-476222" srcset="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/eruo-2.jpg 2000w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/eruo-2-640x364.jpg 640w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/eruo-2-960x546.jpg 960w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/eruo-2-768x437.jpg 768w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/eruo-2-1536x873.jpg 1536w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 2000px) 100vw, 2000px" /><figcaption class="wp-element-caption">Rubio &amp; del Amo and Cruz más Cruz</figcaption></figure>

		<item>
		<title>&#8216;Colorstruck!&#8217; Examines the Connection Between Race and Chromatic Expression</title>
		<link>https://www.thisiscolossal.com/2026/07/richard-j-powell-black-american-art-colorstruck/</link>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Grace Ebert]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Mon, 27 Jul 2026 20:26:58 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Art]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Books]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[History]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[art history]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[color]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[identity]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[painting]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[portraits]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://www.thisiscolossal.com/?p=476206</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[<p><img src="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/colorstruck-2.jpg" alt="&#8216;Colorstruck!&#8217; Examines the Connection Between Race and Chromatic Expression" />'Colorstruck! Painting, Pigment, Affect' delves into the ways that color and social, political, and cultural forces intersect in Black American art.</p>
<p>Do stories and artists like this matter to you? Become a <a href="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/members">Colossal Member</a> today and support independent arts publishing for as little as $7 per month. The article <a href="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/2026/07/richard-j-powell-black-american-art-colorstruck/">&#8216;Colorstruck!&#8217; Examines the Connection Between Race and Chromatic Expression</a> appeared first on <a href="https://www.thisiscolossal.com">Colossal</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<img src="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/colorstruck-2.jpg" alt="&#8216;Colorstruck!&#8217; Examines the Connection Between Race and Chromatic Expression" />


<p>A nude Black woman lies on a stark white chaise, her head propped up by her thin arm. She&#8217;s surrounded by flat, abstracted color in the form of fruits and fabrics, and a glass coupe and bottle on a nearby table offer a clear, rather than refracted, view of the vibrant scene. Rendered in oil on burlap, the painting by William H. Johnson is commanding in its palette and subject matter and an exemplary work in a new book by art historian <a href="https://richardjpowell.com/" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">Richard J. Powell</a>.</p>



<p>Forthcoming this fall from Princeton University Press, <a href="https://bookshop.org/a/96/9780691285160" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener"><em>Colorstruck! Painting, Pigment, Affect</em></a> delves into the ways that color and social, political, and cultural forces intersect in Black American art. Powell takes an expansive approach to each of the three topics—painting, pigment, and affect—and examines works by a wide group of artists, including Jacob Lawrence, Alma Thomas, <a href="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/tags/lorna-simpson/">Lorna Simpson</a>, <a href="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/tags/jean-michel-basquiat/">Jean-Michel Basquiat</a>, and <a href="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/tags/nina-chanel-abney/">Nina Chanel Abney</a>. His interest is in the dynamic interplay of paint and pigment and what the two reveal about both the artists and the viewers.</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-full"><img loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="2000" height="1514" src="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/colorstruck-3.jpg" alt="a stylized painted portrait of a nude Black woman" class="wp-image-476210" srcset="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/colorstruck-3.jpg 2000w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/colorstruck-3-640x484.jpg 640w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/colorstruck-3-960x727.jpg 960w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/colorstruck-3-768x581.jpg 768w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/colorstruck-3-1536x1163.jpg 1536w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 2000px) 100vw, 2000px" /><figcaption class="wp-element-caption">William H. Johnson, &#8220;Nude&#8221; (c. 1939), oil on burlap, 29 ¾ x 38 ¼ inches. Image courtesy of Smithsonian American Art Museum and Art Resource</figcaption></figure>



<p>Sharing a root with words like awestruck or starstruck, <em>colorstruck</em> is a slang term that evolved from &#8220;a Black person who preferred associating with light-skinned Blacks or White people to anyone inordinately preoccupied with race,&#8221; Powell writes. The idea is largely associated with colorism, although in his view, it can also be applied to the ways we marvel at and can even be overwhelmingly affected by an artist&#8217;s palette. He adds: </p>



<blockquote class="wp-block-quote is-layout-flow wp-block-quote-is-layout-flow">
<p>What if a painter, like early Black modernist Willian H. Johnson, set aside the more pejorative insinuations in the idea of being <em>colorstruck</em>, and instead used the paint medium, an intense color palette, racial Blackness, and most important, his abstracting inclinations to produce an expressionistic, evocative, and disruptive work of art? </p>
</blockquote>



<p>The book continues in this line of thinking as it connects what is often thought of as a universal concept—that color exists, and humans respond to certain hues in particular ways—and the distinct context of race in America. Richly illustrated with archival photographs and numerous artworks, the volume captures the relationship between the unique experience of an artist and her viewer and the broader powers that inform those dynamics.</p>



<p><em>Colorstruck! Painting, Pigment, Affect</em> will be published in September, and you can pre-order your copy through <a href="https://bookshop.org/a/96/9780691285160" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">Bookshop</a>.</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-full"><img loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="2000" height="2733" src="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/colorstruck-1.jpg" alt="an abstract print" class="wp-image-476208" srcset="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/colorstruck-1.jpg 2000w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/colorstruck-1-640x875.jpg 640w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/colorstruck-1-960x1312.jpg 960w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/colorstruck-1-768x1049.jpg 768w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/colorstruck-1-1124x1536.jpg 1124w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/colorstruck-1-1499x2048.jpg 1499w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 2000px) 100vw, 2000px" /><figcaption class="wp-element-caption">Hervé Télémaque, &#8220;Négrerie (Black cultural effects)&#8221; (1974), lithograph, 30 x 22 inches. 		<item>
		<title>Dynamic Scenes Emerge from Fumiaki Aono&#8217;s Wooden Assemblages</title>
		<link>https://www.thisiscolossal.com/2026/07/fumiaki-aono-wood-furniture-sculptures/</link>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Grace Ebert]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Mon, 27 Jul 2026 15:49:19 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Art]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[assemblage]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[found objects]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Fumiaki Aono]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[sculpture]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[wood]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://www.thisiscolossal.com/?p=476184</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[<p><img src="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/aono-13.jpg" alt="Dynamic Scenes Emerge from Fumiaki Aono&#8217;s Wooden Assemblages" />Dressers, chests, and cabinets stack into towering assemblages in Fumiaki Aono's imaginative sculptures.</p>
<p>Do stories and artists like this matter to you? Become a <a href="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/members">Colossal Member</a> today and support independent arts publishing for as little as $7 per month. The article <a href="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/2026/07/fumiaki-aono-wood-furniture-sculptures/">Dynamic Scenes Emerge from Fumiaki Aono&#8217;s Wooden Assemblages</a> appeared first on <a href="https://www.thisiscolossal.com">Colossal</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<img src="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/aono-13.jpg" alt="Dynamic Scenes Emerge from Fumiaki Aono&#8217;s Wooden Assemblages" />


<p>Since 1998, <a href="https://aono-fumiaki.com/" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">Fumiaki Aono</a> has been interested in how objects circulate and what happens when they appear in new contexts. Questions of restoration and regeneration naturally followed, and wood became a prime medium for exploring these themes.</p>



<p>Today, Aono continues to revitalize found objects, particularly discarded furniture. Dressers, chests, and cabinets stack into towering assemblages and become the imaginative backdrop for the artist&#8217;s constructed scenes. Converted drawers appear like apartment buildings on a summer day, with tenants leaning out windows and hanging out at street level. Several works also depict box trucks and other vehicles emerging from wooden furnishings, while bicycles, hats, and shoes jut from the edges of sculptures to convey a sense of movement and evolution.</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-full"><img loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="2000" height="2565" src="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/aono-8.jpg" alt="a wooden assemblage sculpture by Fumiaki Aono of two figures carrying furniture" class="wp-image-476196" srcset="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/aono-8.jpg 2000w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/aono-8-640x821.jpg 640w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/aono-8-960x1231.jpg 960w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/aono-8-768x985.jpg 768w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/aono-8-1198x1536.jpg 1198w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/aono-8-1597x2048.jpg 1597w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 2000px) 100vw, 2000px" /></figure>



<p>After experimenting with plywood and timber, Aono&#8217;s transition to secondhand furniture added a conceptual layer to the pieces. These objects &#8220;brought the old memories and lived histories of people into the imagery of the work. In recent years, my concept of &#8216;regeneration&#8217; has evolved beyond mere physical form; it has become a highly complex and multifaceted process encompassing history, memory, ancient legends, and the deep psyche,&#8221; he says.</p>



<p>Explore more from the artist on <a href="https://aono-fumiaki.com/">his website</a> and <a href="https://www.instagram.com/aono_fumiaki/" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">Instagram</a>.</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-full"><img loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="2000" height="2243" src="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/aono-3.jpg" alt="a wooden assemblage sculpture by Fumiaki Aono of a figure peeking out from behind a bookshelf with small scenes" class="wp-image-476188" srcset="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/aono-3.jpg 2000w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/aono-3-640x718.jpg 640w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/aono-3-960x1077.jpg 960w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/aono-3-768x861.jpg 768w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/aono-3-1370x1536.jpg 1370w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/aono-3-1826x2048.jpg 1826w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 2000px) 100vw, 2000px" /></figure>

		<item>
		<title>Damien Aubin Documents a Former Soviet Mining Settlement Suspended in Time</title>
		<link>https://www.thisiscolossal.com/2026/07/damien-aubin-pyramiden-photo-book/</link>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Grace Ebert]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Fri, 24 Jul 2026 18:45:46 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Books]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[History]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Photography]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Damien Aubin]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[landscapes]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Soviet Union]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://www.thisiscolossal.com/?p=476144</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[<p><img src="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/aubin-2.jpg" alt="Damien Aubin Documents a Former Soviet Mining Settlement Suspended in Time" />"The place has not been abandoned. It has been left in suspension," Damien Aubin says.</p>
<p>Do stories and artists like this matter to you? Become a <a href="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/members">Colossal Member</a> today and support independent arts publishing for as little as $7 per month. The article <a href="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/2026/07/damien-aubin-pyramiden-photo-book/">Damien Aubin Documents a Former Soviet Mining Settlement Suspended in Time</a> appeared first on <a href="https://www.thisiscolossal.com">Colossal</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<img src="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/aubin-2.jpg" alt="Damien Aubin Documents a Former Soviet Mining Settlement Suspended in Time" />


<p>The small settlement of <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyramiden" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">Pyramiden</a> on the Norwegian archipelago of Svalbard is literally frozen in time. A former mining outpost for the Soviet Union, industrial operations ceased in 1998, and residents relocated. It wasn&#8217;t until 2007 that a handful of new inhabitants made the settlement home.</p>



<p>Because Pyramiden was abandoned in a cold climate, it remains impeccably preserved, with remnants of its once-thriving settlement still visible. French photographer <a href="https://www.damienaubin.fr/" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">Damien Aubin</a> visited the Arctic region and documented the still, serene environment blanketed in snow. &#8220;The place has not been abandoned. It has been left in suspension,&#8221; he says. </p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-full"><img loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="2000" height="1500" src="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/aubin-8.jpg" alt="a 1990s era classroom" class="wp-image-476157" srcset="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/aubin-8.jpg 2000w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/aubin-8-640x480.jpg 640w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/aubin-8-960x720.jpg 960w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/aubin-8-768x576.jpg 768w, https://www.thisiscolossal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/aubin-8-1536x1152.jpg 1536w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 2000px) 100vw, 2000px" /><figcaption class="wp-element-caption">Classroom, Pyramiden</figcaption></figure>



<p>Pyramiden&#8217;s buildings and the objects inside are largely unchanged. Books sit open on school desks, and an unblemished statue of Lenin presides over a common area. Outside, a towering outdoor monument soars into the sky, the vibrant red and blue paint a stark contrast to the otherwise white landscape. </p>



<p>&#8220;I photograph these environments at a distance, in a restrained, diffuse light. There is no event to describe, no narrative to unfold,&#8221; Aubin adds. &#8220;Across Pyramiden, Barentsburg and Longyearbyen, the same condition appears:<br>spaces shaped by human intent, no longer aligned with it.&#8221;</p>



<p>Aubin has compiled the photos in a limited-edition book slated for release in September. You can purchase a copy on <a href="https://www.damienaubin.fr/pyramiden-book-pre-order" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">his website</a>.</p>
